turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come through, I'll get your observations down before the doctor. Arm out for the cuff, please.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, all right. Make it quick, I'm tired and that waiting room was doing my head in.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 76, oxygen 96 percent, temperature 36.8. I'll pass those to Dr Shah.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The cuff nearly took the arm off, same as every time. Hurry up, would you.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry. Is that Webster pack on the chair yours?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): My daughter's doing. She lives with me and she runs the pills. I stay out of the box or she bites my head off.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Shah. I've seen the observations. What's been the problem?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): These legs. Puffed right up. And I'm exhausted, properly exhausted.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Both sides, or worse on one?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Both. Ankles, and the shins too if I've been standing at the sink.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have the ankles been swollen?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't date it. Last winter, or the one before. Don't keep on about dates.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right. Are you breathless as well, or mainly tired?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Both. Tired all day, and I'm puffed just walking to the letterbox. Have to stop and hang on the gate.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain on that walk?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I'd have said if there was.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): What about a cough, or fevers at home?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. I feel cold of an evening sometimes, but I'm not feverish.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is one calf hotter or redder than the other?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Same both sides. Just fat and shiny.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Passing urine much as usual?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, fine. Do we have to tour the whole body?
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll stick to the medicines. Has anyone been pushing extra tablets on you?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): My sister. She's on biotin for her hair and she keeps at me to take it. It's hers, not mine, so don't you write it down.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Biotin stays off your list. In your own words, what's in the pack?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Water tablet in the morning, and a little white one for the heart — no, I don't know the name. And the blood pressure tablet. She's put that one in twice, I'm telling you, the same tablet.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): The water tablet first. Name and strength?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Frusemide. My daughter says twenty milligrams. I swallow what's in the cup, that's all.
[SEG0029] person_1 (NURSE): The blister is printed frusemide forty milligrams, one each morning. That's this week's pack.

[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): So twenty from your daughter, forty on the label. I won't pretend I know which dose has actually been going in. We'll set a clear dose shortly. The little white one — any writing on it?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Little, white, round. She says it's for the heart. I can't give you a name and I won't make one up.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then we leave it as a little white heart tablet until she brings the names. The one you say is counted twice?

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Perindopril, four milligrams. It's in the morning slot and the same tablet again at lunch, separate cup. I said that's double and she reckons the hospital wanted it. I got sick of the argument.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Perindopril four milligrams is one drug. Morning and lunch means it's been doubled, not two different tablets. When did the lunchtime cup start?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No idea. Since the grand final, or after. Weeks, months, don't ask me to pick.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Timing stays vague, then. Did another doctor stop something?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Spironolactone. The hospital doctor took me off it. Last winter, or the one before. Same answer, I can't pin the date.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): A reason, if you remember?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Potassium, on a blood test. It's stopped. I haven't touched it since.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other regular medicine of yours?

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): That's mine done. My husband takes metformin for his sugar — that's him, keep it off me. I haven't got diabetes. Blood pressure I've had for years, and they say the pump's weak.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll say it back. Blood pressure for years, a weak pump — the heart failure you've been treated for — and no diabetes of your own; husband's metformin and your sister's biotin are not yours. Ankles swollen since last winter or the one before, tired, puffed at the letterbox, no chest pain, no cough, no fever. Frusemide unclear between twenty and forty milligrams, little white heart tablet unnamed, perindopril four milligrams morning and lunch, spironolactone stopped — anything missing?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No. That's the lot. Can you look at the legs and be done? I'm worn out.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Both ankles pit, up to about mid-shin. Calves soft, not hot. Chest clear, no crackles. The pulse feels regular.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. So what is it, and change something. Don't just nod at me.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): My working impression is fluid building up again, with the heart trouble behind it, not a new diagnosis. I'll change the frusemide to forty milligrams in the morning and forty milligrams at lunch, and forget the twenty. Perindopril is four milligrams once in the morning only, so the lunchtime one comes out. Leave the little white one alone until we know its name.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Two water tablets, morning and lunch. One perindopril. Don't touch the white one. Write it down or my daughter won't have a bar of it.

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Script, and a note for her. I also want bloods for the kidneys and potassium, seeing we've moved the water tablet and spironolactone came off because of potassium. Can you take those today, nurse?
[SEG0049] person_1 (NURSE): Yep, I'll do them straight after. Won't take long.

[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in a fortnight either way. If the breathing gets tighter before that, or you can't lie flat, ring us or come straight in, don't wait the fortnight out.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. Fine. Are we done?
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): We're done once the bloods are taken. Go with the nurse, and give that note to your daughter tonight.

spec.situation: Older patient with a live-in carer or daughter who manages the pill box; names of tablets are described ('the little white one', 'the water tablet'), one was stopped by another doctor, one is double-counted. Doctor reviews and changes one medicine.
features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

omissions.text: Family history/social history is recorded wrongly: the transcript says the husband takes metformin for diabetes ('his sugar') and that this is not the patient's condition; this should not be recorded as the patient's family history item 'sugar'.

Frusemide current dose details are incomplete/wrongly captured: the patient reported her daughter says it is 20 mg, while the nurse read the Webster pack label as frusemide 40 mg one each morning, and the doctor explicitly said the actual dose being taken was unclear.
Spironolactone discontinuation reason is missing: it was stopped by a hospital doctor because of high potassium on a blood test, and the patient has not taken it since.
Negative finding missing: urine output/passing urine is unchanged ('passing urine much as usual' / 'fine').
Negative finding missing: no inability to lie flat/orthopnoea was given as a red-flag symptom to seek urgent review if it develops before follow-up.
Examination finding missing: calves were soft as well as not hot.
